editorial:
The Hollywood Revue of 1929 is MGM's attempt to place its entire contract roster on screen in a single feature, produced by Irving Thalberg and Harry Rapf and directed by Charles Reisner. Emceed by Conrad Nagel and Jack Benny, the nearly two-hour revue assembles Joan Crawford, John Gilbert, Norma Shearer, Buster Keaton, Stan Laurel, Oliver Hardy, Lionel Barrymore, Marie Dressler, and more than a dozen other MGM stars in sketches, songs, and specialty acts â€” including the first filmed performance of 'Singin' in the Rain,' delivered by Cliff Edwards. The 1929 photographic print and its synchronized soundtrack entered US public domain on January 1, 2025, when the 95-year maximum copyright term expired.

The practical trap is source selection. Loew's Inc. renewed the copyright in the mid-1950s, keeping the film protected until December 31, 2024, so every pre-2025 commercial release was a licensed copy of protected material. The Warner Archive Collection manufactured-on-demand DVD (ca. 2009) and the Flicker Alley restoration of the Laurel & Hardy magic-act segment on its 'Year Three' Blu-ray both carry new copyright in their transfer and restoration authorship, independent of the underlying 1929 footage. A creator wanting the public-domain print should source from archive.org uploads â€” identifiers the-hollywood-revue-of-1929_1929 and the-hollywood-revue-1929 â€” rather than from rips of those home-video editions.
faq: Is the 'Singin' in the Rain' performance in this film free to use?

The 1929 filmed performance by Cliff Edwards is part of the public-domain print and is free to use as video. The underlying musical composition â€” music by Nacio Herb Brown, lyrics by Arthur Freed, both published in 1929 â€” is also public domain in the US by term expiry. Modern orchestral arrangements, re-recordings, or synchronized scores added to any home-video release are separately protected and must be avoided.
Can I use the Warner Archive DVD as my source copy?

No. The Warner Archive Collection DVD's transfer work carries its own copyright, separate from the 1929 footage. Public-domain status applies to the original 1929 photographic print, not to modern-transfer editions of it. Use archive.org uploads (identifiers: the-hollywood-revue-of-1929_1929 or the-hollywood-revue-1929) as a cleaner source.
